mainEntity.name: How long do dental crowns typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lifespan of a dental crown varies depending on the material used, the location of the crown in the mouth, your oral hygiene habits, and lifestyle factors such as tooth grinding. Many crowns remain functional for ten to fifteen years or longer, whilst others may require replacement sooner. There is no universal guarantee on crown longevity, and individual outcomes differ. Regular dental reviews help to monitor the condition of your crown and identify any issues before they become more significant. Your dentist can provide guidance specific to your situation following a clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can a dental crown fail without causing pain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, it is possible for issues to develop beneath or around a dental crown without causing noticeable pain, particularly in the early stages. Secondary decay forming under a crown, for example, may not produce symptoms until it has progressed significantly. This is one of the key reasons why routine dental reviews — including X-rays where clinically indicated — are important even when patients are not experiencing discomfort. Waiting for pain before seeking a dental assessment is not the most effective approach to protecting your oral health.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if my dental crown falls off?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your dental crown becomes loose or detaches completely, you should contact your dental practice as soon as possible to arrange an urgent appointment. Avoid attempting to reattach the crown yourself using household adhesives. Keep the crown in a safe place and bring it with you to your appointment. In the meantime, avoid chewing on that side of your mouth if possible. The underlying tooth may be sensitive without the crown, so being cautious with temperature extremes in food and drink may help until you are seen by your dentist.

mainEntity.name: Does tooth grinding affect dental crowns?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, bruxism (tooth grinding or clenching) can place significant additional stress on dental crowns, potentially increasing the risk of wear, chipping, or loosening over time. If your dentist identifies signs of tooth grinding during your review, they may recommend a custom-made nightguard to protect your teeth and crowns. This is a preventative measure that many patients find helpful. It is important to raise any concerns about grinding or jaw discomfort with your dentist so that appropriate monitoring and management strategies can be discussed.

mainEntity.name: Will my dental crown need replacing at some point?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most dental crowns will require replacement at some point during a patient's lifetime, though the timing varies significantly depending on the individual circumstances. Your dentist will monitor the condition of your crown during routine reviews and advise you if replacement becomes clinically appropriate. This decision is based on a range of factors, including the structural integrity of the crown, the health of the underlying tooth, and changes in the surrounding gum tissue. No practitioner can predict with certainty how long any individual crown will last, and treatment decisions are always made on a case-by-case basis.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal to feel sensitivity around a dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some degree of sensitivity is common in the days immediately following crown placement as the tooth and surrounding tissues settle. However, if sensitivity persists beyond a few weeks, increases in intensity, or develops new after a period of comfort, this warrants professional assessment. Sensitivity around a crown can have a number of causes, including bite imbalance, gum recession, or changes to the underlying tooth. Your dentist will assess the area to determine the most likely cause and advise on appropriate management. It is always better to have sensitivity investigated than to assume it will resolve on its own.
